hits.name: Argona
hits.text:
i couldn't sleep after reading this

Sam Altman just explained how he uses his own AI agent, and it feels illegal:

he leaves it one long voice note as he's drifting off. by morning the thing is built, and it already "did the next seven steps"

his agent is called Dotty. it sorts the morning fires and only pings him when something is urgent. in his words, it gave him "space for creativity or to just hang out with my kids"

that's literally what openai dots does now. the launch post hit 13.7 million views three days ago. each dot gets its own computer in the cloud, plugs into 4,000+ apps, and you message it inside chatgpt, slack or teams. your laptop stays shut

getting the same morning out of your own dot takes five moves, and the first one matters most:

→ give it one job and keep the chain short. in openai's own safety tests, handing a dot 10 tasks in a row instead of 5 more than doubled the slip-ups
→ write the brief as four answers: what must get done, which sources it reads, what deserves your attention, what it must not do yet
→ skip scheduling the follow-ups. it can "decide when to pause and wake up to continue work", so give it the goal and let it pick its own hours
→ ask for a handful of versions. Altman leaves Dotty notes on how a feature should work and gets several builds back to pick from
→ write repeat jobs like a calendar invite: "every friday at 17:00, post the summary in the team channel. only what's in the summary. ask me first before posting anywhere else"

dots are live on chatgpt pro and business premium, and your first dot comes included in the plan

it learns from your feedback over time. six months from now, the people who started this week will have a dot that knows how they work, and everyone else starts from zero

full playbook in my article below. bookmark this before tonight's voice note

OPENAI JUST SHIPPED AN AGENT THAT DOESN'T WAIT FOR YOUR PROMPT.
it's called a dot. it runs 24/7 on GPT-6 Astra, it has its own cloud computer and browser, it plugs into 4,000+ apps, and it keeps working between your conversations.

Dots are here!

A new way to use AI that works 24/7 for you; get more of your time and attention back to work at a higher level.
Introducing dots
С openai.com
2 тыс.
1 тыс.
14 тыс.
1 млн
every chatbot you've used so far had the same shape. you type, it answers, and it forgets you exist until you type again.
dots break that shape. you hand one a job, you close your laptop, and the job keeps moving.
OpenAI's own framing: a dot gets almost everything you'd give a new hire. an account. a computer. a browser. access to the apps you approve. and a memory that gets sharper every time you correct it.
that changes which skill matters. prompting was about writing one good message. running a dot is about designing a job: what it owns, what it reads, what it may do alone, and when it has to come back to you.
i call that dots engineering. this is the full guide in 10 steps, built from the launch post, the help center and OpenAI's dots docs. no hype. how the thing actually works, and how to set it up so it earns its seat
WHY DOTS ARE NOT JUST ANOTHER AGENT
four things show up at once, and that combination is what's new:
it works between conversations. it tracks progress, works out the next step and follows through as things change. it even decides when to pause and when to wake up again it acts before you ask. OpenAI calls it proactive research: the dot reads what you've connected, keeps private notes and brings you suggestions. those background tools can't send messages, change your apps or drive a browser it manages its own workers. background agents run in parallel and report back to it, and you can keep talking to your dot the whole time it lives where you already are. the same dot answers in ChatGPT, Slack, Teams, on a call or by text, with one memory behind all of them
according to the launch post, the payoff is a dot bringing you work finished the way you would have finished it, before you thought to ask.
it's already happening inside OpenAI:
an error lands in Slack, and dots start hunting for the cause a new design shows up, and dots turn it into a working app while the team reads customer feedback a planning cycle starts, and dots keep the teams on schedule outside OpenAI, an early tester forgot to invoice a publication. the dot noticed, drafted the invoice and sent it once it was approved
that last one is the whole pitch in one line. nobody asked. the dot saw a gap, did the work, and stopped at the approval.

the rollout is gradual. even on an eligible plan it can take a few days to show up in your account. check the current list before you upgrade a plan just for this.

One Prompt, 12 Hours: What Actually Builds the Opus 5.5 Motion Videos

A founder paid over $1,000 for a launch video last year. This September he made the same kind of clip in under 30 minutes.
His caption can honestly say "one prompt". Plenty of other captions say it too, and behind those sit a brief of 9,500 characters, a skills folder, a pair of API keys and 12 hours of unattended running.
Claude Opus 5.5 shipped on September 22, 2026. Anthropic pitched it as matching Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5. Within hours the feed had a new genre: showreels, product launch films, music videos, even history films running five minutes, and every one of them was code rendered into video. The replies wrote motion designers off.
Below is the full pipeline behind those clips, pieced together from the nine posts that set the trend. Rule of thumb: the prompt is 10% of a finished video and the pipeline around the model is the other 90%. So the pipeline comes first, directing second, selling last.
1/ What "one prompt" leaves out
Each side of the argument has half of it. A few of the viral clips did start from a prompt of 30 words. Others had the full production from the intro behind them.
Thariq, who works on Claude Code, turned the gap into a joke about two halves of the same post. The caption claims a one-shot, and the prompt underneath is 10k characters of good takes with skills, examples and API keys attached.
One creator went the other way and published the bill for a 45-second hand-painted watercolor short, stating plainly that it was not a one-shot:
62.7M tokens, 96% of them cache reads
163 model calls
about $34 at API list price
about 6¾ hours start to finish, roughly 1½ of them hands-on
a 12-minute render on a laptop
Their verdict: good cold, and it still needs a proper project around it.
Skip that project and you get the default video: a title in the middle of a gradient, a fade on every element, and a logo to close. The same three things are missing each time. There is no reference, no render engine, and nobody asked the model to check its own frames.
2/ Opus has no video output, so it writes code that draws one
Text and images go into Opus 5.5 and text comes out. An MP4 is not on the menu. Every clip in this wave is a program the model wrote, and a second tool turned that program into pixels.
The whole method rests on one function. Opus names it draw(t) or seek(t), and its only job is to return the correct picture for whatever timestamp it receives. A headless browser calls it once per frame and screenshots the result. ffmpeg stitches the stills.
15 s × 60 fps = 900 frames. Zero timers.
No frame waits on a clock, so two renders of the same file match, and a revision means changing one line and rendering again.
Developer Tommy Rossi took a one-shot output apart and found the model's preferred route has no dependencies at all. Everything lives in one index.html. Playwright opens it in a headless window and evals the seek function for each frame in turn, and ffmpeg encodes the captures into an MP4. For the audio it ran Python, printed the beat timestamps and pasted them into the page as constants. Remotion and HyperFrames were available and went unused.
By his read the code is spaghetti full of magic numbers, a by-product of the video the model already had in mind. So if you want a framework, ask for it by name.
3/ The install: a shell, a browser, ffmpeg
# base tools (Node 22 or newer; Python is for audio)
brew install node ffmpeg python        # Linux: the same packages through apt
pip install numpy librosa soundfile

# an empty project and a headless Chromium
mkdir reel-lab && cd reel-lab
npm init -y
npm i -D playwright
npx playwright install chromium

# route B only: framework skills
npx skills add remotion-dev/skills
npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

# optional plugin: hand-drawn look, with pens, rigs and code-made sound effects
claude plugin marketplace add buildwithhanif/claude-animation-skill
claude plugin install claude-animation@claude-animation-skill

# start the agent on Opus 5.5, then raise the effort from /model
claude --model claude-opus-5-5
Then set the effort. Out of the box Opus 5.5 runs at medium, with thinking always on. None of the viral one-shots used that default. All of them ran on xhigh or max.

hits.text:
OpenAI just showed a system called dots that stops answering questions and starts marking where the answer would have to come from.

It returns no text. It returns points on your own data, each one a place the claim is either supported or is standing on nothing.

> SPREAD - the question broken into the individual claims an answer would need
> ANCHOR - each claim pinned to the exact span in your documents that carries it
> VOID - claims with no span behind them left empty instead of being filled in
> LINK - anchors connected where one claim depends on another holding first
> READ - the finished map returned as points, never as a paragraph

A normal answer hides its own gaps. The sentences are smooth, and the part with nothing underneath reads identically to the rest.

Dots refuses that trade. An unsupported claim shows up as an empty point, impossible to skim past.

The dependency links are the sharp part. One hollow anchor exposes every claim resting on top of it at once.

That turns a wrong answer into a located problem. You see which document is missing, not just that something feels off.

Fluency has been doing the convincing in every tool shipped so far. Here it has nothing to hide behind.

The dot format and how the voids are scored are laid out in the breakdown below.

25-40% of model calls in any agent loop with a review step are checks

who owns which job:
> read a diff, write a review - Claude
> does this pass, is this the right file - Jev

> merge, retry or flag a person - Jev
> enforce the exact rule - your own code

the numbers:
> 348 ms per check
> 93.3% of broken rules caught
> TypeSafe's best case: 200x faster, 400x cheaper

the playbook:
1. audit one real transcript and mark every yes-or-no moment
2. write the schema down: questions, answers, confidence lines
3. move one decision first, keep the rest of the loop as is
4. below the threshold, hand it back to Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.1
5. npx skills add typesafe-ai/skills --skill typesafe-ai

3,778,756 views on his post by Oct 1. 1,628 GitHub stars on the source repo.

> LOGLINE: the film in one line, plus the joke, and every later decision gets checked against it.
> REFERENCES: source video, song, image library, repo. Keep the grammar, never the content.
> TOOLS & KEYS: skills, image, video and voice APIs, a budget of about $2,000 in credits, and an order to spend it economically.
> CHARACTER BIBLE: proportions, palette, expressions, and an identity lock.
> BEAT SHEET: acts with timestamps, a hook in the first 2 seconds, a payoff every 3 to 5 seconds.
> TEXT ON SCREEN: when the lyrics go huge and when they sit like subtitles.
> WORKFLOW GATES: eight checkpoints from plan to final render (rig, stills and animatic first, then the full pass, polish and audio), none skipped.
> CRITIQUE LOOP: stills get rendered and scored, the three weakest spots get fixed, and the cycle runs until nothing scores under 8.
> DELIVERABLES: the finished MP4 plus a poster frame, a contact sheet, a loop check and clean source with a README.

While he slept, the AI reportedly rendered base shots with a video model, redrew the entire video in JavaScript, wrote its own guide file to brief parallel subagents, and delivered 142 seconds at roughly 5 minutes of machine work per finished second.

Viewers only ever see the code-drawn layer.

1. Keep the nine headings.

3. Leave the gates and the 8+ bar alone.
4. Go to bed.

No f*cking way, I just built this web crawler from one single prompt with Opus 5.5

it can:
- follow your cursor across any page
- crawl the text and glitch every word it steps on
- pull out the key sentences as it walks
- build a short TL;DR in real time while you scroll
- take any article you paste in and do the same

here is the prompt: 

Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "TL;DR Crawler" that works on any normal web page.

WHAT IT DOES
Click the toolbar icon: a line-drawn spider appears on the current page, follows your cursor (also while scrolling), reads the text it walks over and builds a short TL;DR in a floating panel. Click the icon again: everything disappears and the page is exactly as before.

1. TOGGLE
- background.js: chrome.action.onClicked injects content.js with chrome.scripting.executeScript.
- content.js checks a global flag. If the crawler is already running, it shuts down and cleans up. Otherwise it starts. Only one instance per tab, ever.

2. FIND THE TEXT
- Find the main readable area: prefer <article> or <main>, otherwise the element with the most paragraph text. Skip nav, header, footer, aside, menus, forms, code, ads and hidden elements.
- Collect text blocks (p, li, blockquote, h2-h4) and split them into sentences. Store each sentence as a DOM Range (sentences can span links and bold text, so do NOT wrap them in elements).
- Watch the area with a debounced MutationObserver (1s) to pick up text loaded later (infinite scroll, lazy content).

3. PICK KEY SENTENCES
- Score each sentence: +2 digits, +2 for %, $, €, million, billion; +1.5 for words like first, record, launch, announce, new, only, biggest, fastest, warns, raises, cuts; +0.3 per capitalized name (max +2); -2 if under 40 or over 260 characters.
- Mark the top 25% as key sentences (min 5, max 80), spread so most paragraphs get one.
- Summaries, max 9 words each:
  - If an API key is set: send all key sentences in ONE request to Claude and ask for a JSON array of short, plain summaries (max 9 words, keep numbers and names exactly, no hype). Request again in batches when new text appears.
  - Without a key: fallback summary = the sentence with filler openers removed (and, but, however, also, according to), cut at a word boundary with "…".

4. THE SPIDER
- Shadow DOM host at document root containing a full-screen fixed <canvas> (pointer-events: none, z-index 2147483646) and the panel.
- Look: small rounded-rectangle body, abdomen ellipse, head with two white eyes, outlines in #5ab8ff. 8 legs as 3px blue lines with pink (#ff4f7a) joint dots, two segments each with inverse kinematics, knees bending outward.
- Gait: two alternating leg groups. A foot steps only when it's ~80px from its ideal spot and the other group is planted. Steps last 0.13s with a small lift, landing slightly ahead in the walking direction.
- Movement: target = cursor position + scroll, so it follows while scrolling. Max ~420 px/s, smooth acceleration, stops ~40px from the cursor, turns smoothly toward its direction. If the cursor is idle for 8s, it wanders around the viewport.
- requestAnimationFrame with a fixed 1/120s physics step. Support devicePixelRatio and window resize.

5. CRAWLING
- Every 80ms and on every foot landing, find the text under the spider with document.caretRangeFromPoint (ignore the extension's own elements).
- If that point is inside a key sentence not yet found: highlight it with the CSS Custom Highlight API (::highlight(tldr-found) with a soft yellow background) and add its summary to the panel.
- If a foot lands on a normal word: in ~25% of cases glitch just that word. Wrap only that word in a span (it's a single text node, so it's safe) and apply one random effect: monospace font, blue outline, blue highlight, slight rotation, wide letter-spacing, blur or uppercase. Max 2 effects per word. Record every change so it can be undone.

6. PANEL
- Top-right, draggable by its header, inside the Shadow DOM so site CSS can't affect it.
- Dark (#16181c), mono title "TL;DR" in yellow (#ffd166), a "found / total" counter, a pink progress bar and a numbered list in article order. The newest item flashes yellow and the list auto-scrolls to it. The list scrolls inside a max height.
- Buttons: "Copy TL;DR" (plain text to the clipboard), "Restart" (clears highlights, glitches and the list) and "Close" (full shutdown).
- If a key is set, add "Write TL;DR with Claude": sends all found sentences and returns 3 short lines using only their facts, numbers unchanged. Show a "Thinking..." state, then the answer under the list.

7. API KEY
- options.html: a field for the user's Anthropic API key and a model name, stored in http://chrome.storage.local.
- All API calls go through background.js with fetch to https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages, with headers x-api-key, anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and content-type: application/json.
- Handle errors quietly: if a call fails, keep the fallback summaries and show a small "AI unavailable" note.

8. QUALITY RULES
- Never break scrolling, clicks, links or text selection on the site.
- Full cleanup on shutdown: canvas, panel, highlights, wrapped word spans, inline styles, listeners, observers, timers.
- prefers-reduced-motion: no glitches, slower walking.
- Plain JavaScript, no libraries. Files: manifest.json, background.js, content.js, options.html, options.js, icons (16, 48, 128).
- Permissions: activeTab, scripting, storage. Host permission: https://api.anthropic.com*.

At the end, give install steps: open chrome://extensions, enable Developer mode, click "Load unpacked", select the folder, then open options and paste the API key.

here is the prompt: 

Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "TL;DR Crawler" that works on any normal web page.

Click the toolbar icon: a line-drawn spider appears on the current page, follows your cursor (also while scrolling), reads the text it walks over and builds a short TL;DR in a floating panel. Click the icon again: everything disappears and the page is exactly as before.

- Collect text blocks (p, li, blockquote, h2-h4) and split them into sentences. Store each sentence as a DOM Range (sentences can span links and bold text, so do NOT wrap them in elements).
- Watch the area with a debounced MutationObserver (1s) to pick up text loaded later (infinite scroll, lazy content).

outsiders.name: Anatoli Kopadze
outsiders.text:
No f*cking way, I just built this web crawler from one single prompt with Opus 5.5

it can:
- follow your cursor across any page
- crawl the text and glitch every word it steps on
- pull out the key sentences as it walks
- build a short TL;DR in real time while you scroll
- take any article you paste in and do the same

here is the prompt: 

Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "TL;DR Crawler" that works on any normal web page.

WHAT IT DOES
Click the toolbar icon: a line-drawn spider appears on the current page, follows your cursor (also while scrolling), reads the text it walks over and builds a short TL;DR in a floating panel. Click the icon again: everything disappears and the page is exactly as before.

1. TOGGLE
- background.js: chrome.action.onClicked injects content.js with chrome.scripting.executeScript.
- content.js checks a global flag. If the crawler is already running, it shuts down and cleans up. Otherwise it starts. Only one instance per tab, ever.

2. FIND THE TEXT
- Find the main readable area: prefer <article> or <main>, otherwise the element with the most paragraph text. Skip nav, header, footer, aside, menus, forms, code, ads and hidden elements.
- Collect text blocks (p, li, blockquote, h2-h4) and split them into sentences. Store each sentence as a DOM Range (sentences can span links and bold text, so do NOT wrap them in elements).
- Watch the area with a debounced MutationObserver (1s) to pick up text loaded later (infinite scroll, lazy content).

3. PICK KEY SENTENCES
- Score each sentence: +2 digits, +2 for %, $, €, million, billion; +1.5 for words like first, record, launch, announce, new, only, biggest, fastest, warns, raises, cuts; +0.3 per capitalized name (max +2); -2 if under 40 or over 260 characters.
- Mark the top 25% as key sentences (min 5, max 80), spread so most paragraphs get one.
- Summaries, max 9 words each:
  - If an API key is set: send all key sentences in ONE request to Claude and ask for a JSON array of short, plain summaries (max 9 words, keep numbers and names exactly, no hype). Request again in batches when new text appears.
  - Without a key: fallback summary = the sentence with filler openers removed (and, but, however, also, according to), cut at a word boundary with "…".

4. THE SPIDER
- Shadow DOM host at document root containing a full-screen fixed <canvas> (pointer-events: none, z-index 2147483646) and the panel.
- Look: small rounded-rectangle body, abdomen ellipse, head with two white eyes, outlines in #5ab8ff. 8 legs as 3px blue lines with pink (#ff4f7a) joint dots, two segments each with inverse kinematics, knees bending outward.
- Gait: two alternating leg groups. A foot steps only when it's ~80px from its ideal spot and the other group is planted. Steps last 0.13s with a small lift, landing slightly ahead in the walking direction.
- Movement: target = cursor position + scroll, so it follows while scrolling. Max ~420 px/s, smooth acceleration, stops ~40px from the cursor, turns smoothly toward its direction. If the cursor is idle for 8s, it wanders around the viewport.
- requestAnimationFrame with a fixed 1/120s physics step. Support devicePixelRatio and window resize.

5. CRAWLING
- Every 80ms and on every foot landing, find the text under the spider with document.caretRangeFromPoint (ignore the extension's own elements).
- If that point is inside a key sentence not yet found: highlight it with the CSS Custom Highlight API (::highlight(tldr-found) with a soft yellow background) and add its summary to the panel.
- If a foot lands on a normal word: in ~25% of cases glitch just that word. Wrap only that word in a span (it's a single text node, so it's safe) and apply one random effect: monospace font, blue outline, blue highlight, slight rotation, wide letter-spacing, blur or uppercase. Max 2 effects per word. Record every change so it can be undone.

6. PANEL
- Top-right, draggable by its header, inside the Shadow DOM so site CSS can't affect it.
- Dark (#16181c), mono title "TL;DR" in yellow (#ffd166), a "found / total" counter, a pink progress bar and a numbered list in article order. The newest item flashes yellow and the list auto-scrolls to it. The list scrolls inside a max height.
- Buttons: "Copy TL;DR" (plain text to the clipboard), "Restart" (clears highlights, glitches and the list) and "Close" (full shutdown).
- If a key is set, add "Write TL;DR with Claude": sends all found sentences and returns 3 short lines using only their facts, numbers unchanged. Show a "Thinking..." state, then the answer under the list.

7. API KEY
- options.html: a field for the user's Anthropic API key and a model name, stored in http://chrome.storage.local.
- All API calls go through background.js with fetch to https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages, with headers x-api-key, anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and content-type: application/json.
- Handle errors quietly: if a call fails, keep the fallback summaries and show a small "AI unavailable" note.

8. QUALITY RULES
- Never break scrolling, clicks, links or text selection on the site.
- Full cleanup on shutdown: canvas, panel, highlights, wrapped word spans, inline styles, listeners, observers, timers.
- prefers-reduced-motion: no glitches, slower walking.
- Plain JavaScript, no libraries. Files: manifest.json, background.js, content.js, options.html, options.js, icons (16, 48, 128).
- Permissions: activeTab, scripting, storage. Host permission: https://api.anthropic.com*.

At the end, give install steps: open chrome://extensions, enable Developer mode, click "Load unpacked", select the folder, then open options and paste the API key.
